name: Pace
seoDesc: Pace: work out time from the speed and the distance. A free sports calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Pace calculator turns the speed and the distance into time. That makes it useful for a training session, a performance comparison or a competition result. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Pace calculator work?
sections.html:
The Pace calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports time in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the race distance (Previous race performance) and the units); then you type in the speed and the distance (Estimate the finishing time for your next race).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Pace calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Time=distance ÷ speed
Time=distance × pace
Level (adjusted pace)=(compare to..., adjusted pace, distance, race distance)
Predicted finishing time=(((race distance > 0) ? ( (time, distance, compare to..., distance) ) : ( (time, distance, compare to..., distance) )))
Adjusted pace=((((race distance > 0) ? ( (time, distance, compare to..., distance) ) : ( (time, distance, compare to..., distance) )))) ÷ distance
Table conversion=(((units) ? ( 621371 ÷ 1000000 ) : ( 1 )))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Time, opening in hours / minutes / seconds
  • Run pace, opening in minutes:seconds per kilometer
  • Speed, opening in kilometers per hour
  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Time, opening in hours / minutes / seconds
  • Run pace, opening in minutes:seconds per kilometer

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Pace calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the speed and the distance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Pace calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns time, derived from the speed and the distance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Pace calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the speed and the distance, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter distance (Previous race performance) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Distance (Previous race performance) opens in kilometers and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (5 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Distance = 0 km. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Pace calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
